target.title: feat: add Zed Remote Projects handoff
target.body:
Related: https://github.com/zed-industries/zed/pull/61102

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where users opening a Crabbox workspace in Zed Remote Projects had to assemble the connection workflow themselves: resolve the lease, synchronize the checkout, paste the SSH command, discover the remote folder, and keep the lease active while Zed runs its own SSH processes.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a provider-neutral `crabbox zed` command that reuses the existing SSH target resolution and lease-activity paths. It verifies the current repository's synced remote folder, prints a Zed-compatible SSH command plus the exact folder, and holds the lease activity until Ctrl-C.

The command does not modify `~/.ssh/config` or Zed settings. It rejects Windows remote targets and token-as-username credentials because Zed remote servers support Linux/macOS and editor settings should not persist provider secrets. The emitted executable is unquoted for compatibility with current Zed releases while every SSH argument remains shell-quoted.

## User Impact

Users can now run:

```sh
crabbox run --id <lease> --sync-only
crabbox zed --id <lease>
```

Then paste the printed command into Zed's **Connect New Server** flow, open the printed folder, and keep the command running for lease activity. The configured hard TTL still applies, and stopping the command does not release the lease.

## Evidence

- `go test -race -p 1 ./...`
- `go test ./internal/cli -count=1`
- `go vet ./...`
- `./scripts/check-docs.sh`
- Live local-container acceptance: provisioned a Linux lease, synced 1,510 files (22.9 MiB), emitted a command containing a spaced identity path and the exact remote folder, held the session, exited cleanly on Ctrl-C, and released the lease/container.
- Security/config implications: no credential output for token-auth providers and no persistent SSH or editor configuration changes.

target.title: fix(worker): drain pipes before cmd.Wait to stop stdout truncation
target.body:
fix(worker): own container-runner pipe ends to prevent stdout truncation and exec hangs

## Summary
Give the cloudflare-container-runner exec path **self-owned `os.Pipe()` write-ends** so `cmd.Wait` never closes the read-ends. A long-running foreground command is drained in full (no truncation), and a lingering background descendant that inherited a write-end is bounded by a **drain-until-idle** policy rather than the process's runtime — so exec never hangs and never stalls.

## What to review
| file | change |
|---|---|
| worker/cloudflare-container-runner/main.go | self-owned `os.Pipe()` ends; drain-until-idle (progress counter → 300ms idle close, 5s absolute cap) |
| worker/cloudflare-container-runner/stdout_truncation_test.go | full-output, prompt-return-under-descendant, noisy-descendant-bounded, bursty-idle-reset, long-foreground no-truncation |

## How it works
`runCommand` creates `rOut/wOut`, `rErr/wErr`, sets `cmd.Stdout=wOut`/`cmd.Stderr=wErr`, and after `Start()` closes the parent's write-end copies so only the child and its descendants hold write-ends. The copiers read the parent-owned read-ends, which `cmd.Wait` never touches. Sequence: start copiers → `cmd.Wait` (child may run arbitrarily long; every byte is delivered) → a drain loop that returns instantly on real EOF, else closes the read-ends once (`sync.Once`) after **300ms with no copier progress** (buffered output drained, descendant quiet), bounded by a **5s absolute cap** (a continuously-writing descendant). Zero truncation by construction — the idle timer only fires after progress stops, and a copier blocked in a slow response write (downstream backpressure) is tracked as in-flight rather than idle, so the drain never closes mid-flush.

## Motivation
Fixes stdout truncation. The two prior iterations were correctly rejected: `wg.Wait()` before `cmd.Wait()` introduced an unbounded hang when a background descendant held the inherited pipe (repro `sleep 60 & echo done` → context deadline); a fixed 5s grace then made every such command stall 5s. This drain-until-idle design resolves all three: no truncation, no hang, no stall.

## Testing
- `go build ./...` + `go vet ./...` at repo root and in the runner module; `gofmt` clean.
- `go test -race -run TestRunCommand -count=3 .` (runner module) — green ×3.
- Red→green: the prompt-return assertion (return under `pipeDrainGrace/2`) **fails on the fixed-grace version** (5.1s) and **passes now** (0.55–0.64s). The 1 MiB full-delivery and long-foreground no-truncation guarantees are retained.

## Real-behavior proof
Captured live against the built runner (a standalone HTTP server; no coordinator/lease needed) — base vs this branch:
```
BASE (pre-fix)  1 MiB stream: 1048576/1048576 delivered    sleep 60 & echo done: returned 0.46s, output intact
HEAD (branch)   1 MiB stream: 1048576/1048576 delivered    sleep 60 & echo done: returned 0.80s, output intact
```
The truncation itself is a **race masked by socket buffering** — a slow network client cannot force it (the TCP send buffer + HTTP buffering absorb ~1 MiB before backpressure reaches the copiers), so it does not reproduce as a live base-vs-head differential. The deterministic regression reproduces it directly at the real `runCommand`/`os.Pipe`/subprocess level (base loses 49,152 bytes of 1 MiB; branch delivers all), and this branch eliminates the race by construction. The live capture above confirms the branch delivers full output and returns promptly under a background descendant.

target.title: fix(cli): don't report ctx-killed pond-mesh forwards as failures
target.body:
fix(cli): classify pond-mesh forward failures by per-forward cancellation provenance

## Summary
Stop classifying a forward's `Wait` failure by reading the **shared** `ctx.Err()` — under a race that discards a genuine non-zero exit when a sibling forward (or the caller) cancels first. Classify by **per-forward provenance recorded at the process boundary** instead: a real failure survives teardown, and a clean Ctrl-C reports no spurious tunnel error.

## What to review
| file | change |
|---|---|
| internal/cli/pond_mesh.go | provenance-based classification; default (uncatchable) kill; record `firstErr` only when the exit is not our own teardown |
| internal/cli/pond_mesh_cancel_unix.go | unix: `cancelled && WaitStatus.Signaled()` |
| internal/cli/pond_mesh_cancel_windows.go | windows: `cancelled && !killFoundExited` (a genuine exit that raced cancel is still recorded) |
| internal/cli/pond_mesh_ctx_cancel_test.go / _race_unix_test.go / _test.go | graceful-cancel over the real `ProcessState` (no mock), two-forward genuine-failure race, PID-reap leak check |

## How it works
The ctx-watchdog Cancel hook records provenance (sets `cancelled` before the kill) and performs `exec.CommandContext`'s default kill — **SIGKILL on Unix** (uncatchable, so a torn-down forward is always `Signaled()`) and **TerminateProcess on Windows** (with `killFoundExited` flagging a process that had already exited on its own). A genuine `Exited()` non-zero code is therefore recorded even when the shared context was cancelled first; our own teardown is suppressed.

## Motivation
The prior single `ctx.Err()==nil` guard could swallow a real forward failure under a race, and an intermediate graceful-SIGINT variant misclassified a signal-catching `ssh` (exit 255) as a genuine failure on clean Ctrl-C — both correctly flagged. This design fixes both by never inferring intent from shared state.

## Testing
- `go build`/`go vet` native **and `GOOS=windows`**; `go test -race -count=3 ./internal/cli -run PondMesh` green; full internal/cli `-race` green; `gofmt` clean.
- Red→green: the graceful-cancel test (real runner + a SIGINT-catching fake ssh, no mocked classifier) **fails on the prior approach** (spurious exit 255) and **passes now**; the two-forward genuine-failure test (exit 7 survives a sibling's cancel) passes; PID-reap leak check passes.

## Real-behavior proof
The regression drives the **real** `runPondMeshForwards` + real `pondMeshExecRunner` over real subprocesses (fake `ssh` via PATH), reproducing the base-vs-branch behavior deterministically under `-race`. A live `pond connect` Ctrl-C capture would require a running coordinator and a provisioned pond (≥2 leases); this contribution was developed without coordinator or provider access, so the deterministic reproduction over the real client/runner/process path is the strongest evidence available here. The Windows classifier path is verified by `GOOS=windows` build+vet (the fake-ssh tests are Unix-gated). A maintainer with a coordinator + pond can confirm live if required.

target.title: fix(cli): deliver server-first egress banner racing the CONNECT handshake

fix(cli): deliver the server-first egress banner racing the CONNECT response

## Summary
For a server-first protocol (SSH, SMTP) over mediated egress, buffer the server's opening banner until the local proxy handshake completes, so the client sees `200 Connection Established` immediately followed by an intact banner — without dropping a rejected-open HTTP response.

## What to review
| file | change |
|---|---|
| internal/cli/egress.go | early-register the stream + `notReady` gate + a readiness barrier so server-first bytes are held until the CONNECT `200` is written, then flushed intact; rejected opens still return their HTTP response |
| internal/cli/egress_banner_buffer_test.go | net.Pipe regressions for ordering, the ready path, and the rejection path |

## How it works
On open, the stream is registered before the upstream may emit data; `writeConn` waits on `b.ready` while an id is `notReady`, so a server-first banner is buffered rather than raced against the CONNECT response. Once the local proxy handshake completes and `200 Connection Established` is written, the barrier releases and the banner flushes in order. A rejected open takes the `502` path and its HTTP response is preserved.

## Testing
- `go build ./...` + `go vet` + `go test -race` (internal/cli) green.
- The regressions build the egress bridge and assert (a) `200` strictly precedes an intact banner, (b) the readiness path does not stall multiplexed egress, (c) a rejected open still returns `502`. Fail on the base revision (dropped/re-ordered banner) / pass on this branch.

## Real-behavior proof
The regressions drive the fixed ordering/readiness/rejection logic deterministically over `net.Pipe`. A live capture of a real CONNECT through the coordinator + host bridge to a server-first endpoint would require a running coordinator + provisioned lease; this contribution was developed without coordinator or provider access, so the deterministic reproduction over the real bridge logic is the strongest evidence available here. A maintainer with a coordinator + lease can confirm live (`200` then an intact `SSH-2.0-…` banner, plus a `502` rejected-open) if required.

target.title: fix(cli): lock egress host-daemon starts to prevent double-provision
target.body:
fix(cli): serialize concurrent egress host-daemon starts per lease

## Summary
Two concurrent `egress host --id <lease>` daemon starts for the same lease could each spawn a supervisor, leaving an untracked duplicate. Serialize the start per lease so exactly one live supervisor exists and its PID is the one recorded.

## What to review
| file | change |
|---|---|
| internal/cli/egress.go | per-lease lock around `startEgressHostDaemon` so concurrent starts for one lease are serialized; the loser observes the existing supervisor instead of spawning a second |
| internal/cli/egress_daemon_double_provision_test.go | deterministic two-start race with real child processes |

## How it works
`startEgressHostDaemon` takes a per-lease lock before checking/writing the PID file and spawning the supervisor, so a racing second start blocks, then sees the recorded supervisor and does not double-provision. The PID file and the single live supervisor stay consistent.

## Testing
- `go build ./...` + `go vet` + `go test -race` (internal/cli) green.
- The regression spawns real child processes and drives `startEgressHostDaemon` concurrently for one lease, asserting exactly one live supervisor whose PID matches the pid file. Fails on the base revision (two supervisors) / passes on this branch.

## Not included (scope boundary)
A separate race between a standalone `egress stop` and a concurrent `start` can still orphan a daemon; it is distinct from this concurrent-start fix and is tracked as a follow-up (the clean fix is the same per-lease lock on `stopEgressHostDaemon` via a locked/unlocked split).

## Real-behavior proof
The regression spawns **real** supervisor child processes and reproduces the double-provision base-vs-branch (two supervisors → one). A capture of the built CLI against a real egress lease would require a running coordinator + provisioned lease; this contribution was developed without coordinator or provider access, so the deterministic real-process reproduction is the strongest evidence available here. A maintainer with a coordinator + lease can confirm live (two `egress host` starts → one live supervisor + clean `egress stop`) if required.

| file | change |
|---|---|
| internal/cli/egress.go | client `openRemote` timeout/cancel path: finish the pending open, remove it from the pending map, and signal the host to close the destination conn + its copy goroutine |
| internal/cli/egress_openremote_leak_test.go | regression driving the real client path through the real timeout |

## How it works
On the timeout (`<-timer.C`) or cancel (`<-ctx.Done()`) branch of `openRemote`, the client finishes the open, drops the id from the pending map, and emits the `close` the host already handles (`hostOpen` registers `conns[id]`; a `close` tears down the destination conn + `copyConnToBridge`). The host-side teardown path is pre-existing and unchanged — this fix makes the client actually send that `close` and clean its own pending state.

- The regression drives `connectEgressBridge` + `clientReadLoop` + `openRemote` over a **real** WebSocket through the **real** 20s `egressOpenTimeout` against a blackholed dial, and fails deterministically on the base revision (pending entry + host conn + copy goroutine leak) / passes on this branch.

## Real-behavior proof
The regression exercises the real client code over a real WebSocket; the host peer is faked because a live host requires a running coordinator + provisioned lease. - `go build ./...` + `go vet ./...` at repo root and in the runner module; `gofmt` clean.
- `go test -race -run TestRunCommand -count=3 .` (runner module) — green ×3.
- Red→green: the prompt-return assertion (return under `pipeDrainGrace/2`) **fails on the fixed-grace version** (5.1s) and **passes now** (0.55–0.64s). The 1 MiB full-delivery and long-foreground no-truncation guarantees are retained.

## Real-behavior proof
Captured live against the built runner (a standalone HTTP server; no coordinator/lease needed) — base vs this branch:
```
BASE (pre-fix)  1 MiB stream: 1048576/1048576 delivered    sleep 60 & echo done: returned 0.46s, output intact
HEAD (branch)   1 MiB stream: 1048576/1048576 delivered    sleep 60 & echo done: returned 0.80s, output intact
```
The truncation itself is a **race masked by socket buffering** — a slow network client cannot force it (the TCP send buffer + HTTP buffering absorb ~1 MiB before backpressure reaches the copiers), so it does not reproduce as a live base-vs-head differential. The deterministic regression reproduces it directly at the real `runCommand`/`os.Pipe`/subprocess level (base loses 49,152 bytes of 1 MiB; branch delivers all), and this branch eliminates the race by construction. The live capture above confirms the branch delivers full output and returns promptly under a background descendant.

target.body:
## Summary

- Reframe the Features index around reusable capabilities rather than providers or command syntax.
- Replace the long generated Markdown list with a polished, responsive capability explorer on `/features/`.
- Add a strong product-oriented hero, a Lease → Sync → Run → Prove flow, live search, category filters, result counts, and linked capability cards.
- Keep provider discovery in the canonical Provider Reference and command syntax in the Command Reference.
- Preserve every existing feature document and URL; the enhancement runs after the normal docs build and only transforms the Features landing page.

## Why

The docs now give Providers a first-class section, but the Features landing page still behaved like a dense Markdown inventory and duplicated adjacent information architecture. It was technically complete but difficult to scan, did not communicate the product workflow, and made dozens of capability guides feel flat and undifferentiated.

This change gives `/features/` one clear job: help a reader understand what Crabbox can do and quickly find the relevant capability contract.

## UX and accessibility

- Responsive three-, two-, and one-column card layouts.
- Searchable capability titles and descriptions.
- Filter pills for each capability area, with pressed state and live result counts.
- Keyboard-friendly native links, buttons, labels, and search input.
- Escape clears an active search.
- Empty-result status is announced and category sections hide only when they have no visible cards.
- Existing light/dark theme variables and reduced-motion behavior remain authoritative.
- Provider and command CTAs create an explicit handoff to the correct top-level section.

## Implementation

The shared Markdown renderer remains unchanged. `scripts/enhance-docs-site.mjs` deterministically post-processes only `dist/docs-site/features/index.html` after the normal build. This isolates the richer landing-page treatment from all other documentation pages and avoids committing generated output.

The Pages workflow and `scripts/check-docs.sh` both run the enhancement, so CI validates the same output that is deployed.

## Visual proof

The `Docs UI Proof / Render visual proof` check builds the exact generated docs output from the PR head, runs the enhancer and regression tests, and renders browser screenshots with pinned Playwright/Chromium.

Its downloadable artifact is named `features-ui-proof-<head-sha>` and contains:

- `features-desktop-light.png` — full desktop layout in light mode.
- `features-desktop-dark.png` — full desktop layout using the dark color scheme.
- `features-mobile.png` — full responsive mobile layout using an iPhone viewport.
- `SHA256SUMS` — digests binding each proof image to the workflow artifact.

The proof job also fails unless the generated page contains the capability explorer, product hero, provider handoff, and command-reference handoff. This makes the evidence reproducible rather than a manually edited screenshot.

## Validation

- `node --check scripts/enhance-docs-site.mjs`
- `node --test scripts/enhance-docs-site.test.mjs`
- Enhancer regression coverage verifies the hero, search/filter surface, capability-card generation, TOC/pager removal, idempotence, and no-op behavior for unrelated pages.
- `Docs UI Proof / Render visual proof` publishes desktop light, desktop dark, and mobile screenshots from the exact built PR output.
- Branch is based directly on upstream `main` (`6da7760693a820c53434b4774077f526d362c136`) with no unrelated files.

Generated site output remains uncommitted.
